edbDesc: (sometimes referred to as boiling retardation, or boiling delay) The phenomenon in which a liquid is heated to a temperature higher than its boiling point, without boiling. Superheating is achieved by heating a homogeneous substance in a clean container, free of nucleation sites, while taking care not to disturb the liquid.
title: Superheating
description: Water heated in a very clean, smooth container can rise above its boiling point without boiling, then erupt all at once when disturbed. Donny heated air-free water far past 100 degrees in the 1840s; Glaser later used a superheated liquid to make the bubble chamber, where passing particles leave trails of bubbles.
effect: a liquid heated past its boiling point stays liquid until disturbed
usedIn: Boiling chips and stones that prevent bumping in labs
strength: Water in a smooth mug can pass 100 degrees in a microwave and erupt when a spoon goes in; air-free water has been held liquid above 130 degrees.
pickWhy: Borderline: Specific effect with real uses; I'm unsure of the discoverer and date (Donny 1846 is my best recollection; Deluc noted it in the 1700s).
